title: AI-Assisted Design of a Post-Quantum Cryptographic Accelerator
content:
Computer Science > Cryptography and Security
  [Submitted on 3 Sep 2026]
    Title:AI-Assisted Design of a Post-Quantum Cryptographic Accelerator: A Deployed-Silicon Case Study
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Post-quantum migration is mandated on published timelines, and silicon that ships with a defect cannot be patched remotely. The standard acceptance gate cannot detect an entire class of ML-DSA defects. Signing resamples until a candidate meets its norm bounds, so the executed path varies with the message, whereas known-answer tests (KATs) sample fixed values and reach only the depths their seeds trigger. Our accelerator passed its full KAT regression while carrying a norm check that outran block-RAM latency, leaving each candidate's final coefficients unverified; the escape surfaced at reject-loop iteration 5. The blind spot lies in the instrument, not the engineer; care cannot remove it. We replace that gate. A byte-exact golden-reference oracle paired with randomized adversarial soak drives the rejection loop past any fixed vector, closing the gap: 301,343 data-dependent signings, zero escapes. Because the gate judges artifacts and never authors, trust becomes separable from authorship, making AI authorship an answerable question. We report 232 logged experiments in which an agentic large language model drove a unified ML-KEM-768 and ML-DSA-65 accelerator with on-chip key custody from RTL to PCIe bring-up on one Kintex-7 XC7K160T, shipped at 98.5% slice occupancy. Success was 71.6%, following a hardware-coupling gradient, 77-85% for documentation and research against 50-53% for synthesis and bring-up, which observability can explain: failure concentrates where corrective signals are physical-side only. That so unreliable an author produced an artifact byte-exact across all six FIPS operations -- its deployed baseline surviving the same 779,945-check zero-failure soak -- is the claim.

report.summary: AI agents designed and deployed a post-quantum crypto accelerator, revealing KAT blind spots and validating randomized soak testing.
report.background: Post-quantum migration is scheduled globally, and chips that ship with defects cannot be patched after deployment. The standard acceptance gate for cryptographic silicon, known-answer tests (KATs), samples fixed input vectors. But ML-DSA signs by resampling candidates until norm bounds are satisfied, so execution paths vary with message content. Fixed KAT vectors only reach depths their seeds trigger, leaving a class of defects invisible. In this case, the accelerator passed full KAT regression despite a norm check that outran block-RAM latency, leaving coefficients unverified; the flaw surfaced only at reject-loop iteration 5. The authors argue this is an instrumentation blind spot, not a human engineer error. They replaced the gate with a byte-exact golden-reference oracle plus randomized adversarial soak testing, closing the gap with 301,343 data-dependent signings and zero escapes. This method judges artifacts, not authors, making AI authorship a tractable, verifiable question.
key_points: Standard KATs miss path-dependent bugs in post-quantum algorithms. ML-DSA's rejection sampling creates data-dependent execution flows, and fixed test vectors only probe a shallow subset of possible states, leaving timing- or latency-dependent defects undetected in shipped silicon.

The solution combines a byte-exact golden reference with randomized adversarial soak testing. By driving the rejection loop far beyond fixed vectors, the team found and eliminated the blind spot—301,343 randomized signings produced zero escapes, far stronger evidence than KATs alone.

AI-driven hardware design is unevenly reliable. Across 232 logged experiments, an agentic LLM succeeded 71.6% of the time: 77-85% on documentation and research, but only 50-53% on synthesis and bring-up, where corrective feedback is mostly observable only on the physical side.

Despite the AI author's overall unreliability, the resulting unified ML-KEM-768/ML-DSA-65 accelerator shipped on a Kintex-7 at 98.5% slice occupancy, was byte-exact across all six FIPS operations, and survived a 779,945-check zero-failure soak—showing that verified artifacts can outpace their creator's raw success rate.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this demonstrates that large language models can produce deployable silicon-level cryptographic designs, but reliability is strongly task-dependent and tied to observability. Developers should not assume AI-generated hardware is correct simply because standard tests pass—especially for data-dependent security functions. The findings push verification methodology toward randomized adversarial oracles and artifact-centric trust rather than authorship. For regular users, this bolsters confidence in post-quantum migration security, since rigorous soak testing can catch subtle side-channel or timing defects that fixed-vector tests miss. It also suggests that future hardware design workflows will pair human engineers with AI agents under stronger automated validation, altering how security-critical chips are audited and certified.
report.tools: Practitioners interested in AI-assisted silicon verification should watch Cocotb for Python-based testbenches, Verilator for fast simulation, and OpenTitan as an open-source root-of-trust reference. For post-quantum algorithm validation, PQClean provides portable C implementations with known-answer tests, and the ML-KEM/ML-DSA draft standards themselves include consistency vectors useful for building golden references.
